pages.title: Dungeons & Dragons, 1974
pages.body: Gary Gygax and Dave Arneson wrote the original Dungeons & Dragons. TSR published the boxed set in 1974. Its fantasy rules grew from miniature wargaming.

pages.title: Traveller, 1977
pages.body: Traveller was published in 1977 by Game Designers Workshop. The science-fiction game extended tabletop adventures beyond fantasy settings.

pages.title: RuneQuest, 1978
pages.body: Chaosium introduced RuneQuest in 1978. The game used a percentile system and the fantasy setting Glorantha, with skills instead of character classes and levels.

pages.title: Call of Cthulhu, 1981
pages.body: Chaosium released Call of Cthulhu in 1981. Its horror investigations use a percentile system. This page records the release, not a scenario walkthrough.

pages.title: Tabletop to digital adventures
pages.body: Early computer adventures adapted tabletop play. Donald Daglow described writing Dungeon in the Smithsonian oral-history record. Digital adventures made a computer handle parts of the referee role.

pages.title: Permineralization
pages.body: During permineralization, dissolved minerals in groundwater fill tiny pores in organic remains. The original material can persist while the added minerals help preserve its structure.

pages.title: Trace fossils
pages.body: Trace fossils record biological activity rather than a preserved body part. A footprint impression, a burrow, or a coprolite can preserve evidence of an organism.

pages.title: Molds and casts
pages.body: A mold preserves an impression left by an organism. A cast forms when material fills that cavity, creating a three-dimensional copy of the original shape.

pages.title: Body fossils
pages.body: Body fossils preserve actual parts of organisms, such as bones, shells, or plant material. They differ from evidence of activity left without the organism itself.

pages.title: Amber preservation
pages.body: Entrapment in resin that becomes amber can preserve organisms. Amber preservation is different from filling a bone with minerals; fossils do not all become stone.

pages.title: Mammals
pages.body: Mammals have hair and mammary glands. Milk production is called lactation. These traits help identify mammals even when they live in water or fly.

pages.title: Birds
pages.body: Birds are feathered vertebrates. Modern birds belong to the surviving dinosaur lineage. A backbone places them within vertebrates even though their bodies have many flight adaptations.

pages.title: Insects
pages.body: Adult insects have six legs and three main body regions. Many insects undergo metamorphosis, changing form during development. Insects are invertebrates rather than animals with a backbone.

pages.title: Amphibians
pages.body: Frogs are amphibians. Many frogs undergo metamorphosis from an aquatic tadpole into an adult. Amphibians are vertebrates, alongside fish, reptiles, birds, and mammals.

pages.title: Vertebrate collections
pages.body: Vertebrate zoology studies animals with backbones. Museum collections include fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Invertebrate collections cover animals outside those groups.

pages.title: End-Cretaceous extinction
pages.body: Non-avian dinosaurs disappeared around 66 million years ago. The Chicxulub asteroid impact is associated with the end-Cretaceous mass extinction. Birds survived, so dinosaurs did not vanish entirely.

pages.title: Bird ancestry
pages.body: Birds evolved within the theropod dinosaur lineage. Living birds are therefore dinosaurs. Shared skeletal features and fossil discoveries connect birds to extinct relatives.

pages.title: Tyrannosaurus rex
pages.body: Tyrannosaurus rex was a large theropod with powerful jaws and teeth. The museum skeleton documents its anatomy. This page does not estimate auction values or ownership rights.

pages.title: Sauropods
pages.body: Sauropods included long-necked, long-tailed herbivores such as Apatosaurus. They walked on four limbs. Their body plan differs from the two-legged forms of many meat-eating dinosaurs.

pages.title: Pterosaur boundary
pages.body: Pterosaurs were flying reptiles related to dinosaurs but outside the dinosaur group. Their anatomy differs from the diagnostic features of dinosaurs. Sharing an ancient habitat does not make every reptile a dinosaur.

pages.title: OpenAI introduction, 2015
pages.body: OpenAI announced its formation on December 11, 2015. The announcement described a nonprofit artificial intelligence research organization and its goal of benefiting humanity. This records the historical announcement.

pages.title: GPT-2, 2019
pages.body: OpenAI announced GPT-2 in February 2019. The transformer language model predicted subsequent words. Its initial staged release reflected concerns about misuse of generated text.

pages.title: GPT-3, 2020
pages.body: The 2020 GPT-3 paper studied a transformer language model with 175 billion parameters. It evaluated few-shot tasks using examples supplied in context rather than task-specific fine-tuning.

pages.title: DALL-E, 2021
pages.body: OpenAI introduced DALL-E in January 2021. The model generated images from descriptions, connecting natural-language prompts with visual synthesis. This page describes that original research announcement.

pages.title: ChatGPT, 2022
pages.body: OpenAI introduced ChatGPT on November 30, 2022 as a conversational research preview. The announcement described dialogue, follow-up questions, and learning from user feedback.

pages.title: ENIAC, 1946
pages.body: ENIAC was publicly unveiled in 1946. John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert built the electronic computing system at the University of Pennsylvania. It used vacuum tubes and programming through wiring and switches.

pages.title: Transistor, 1947
pages.body: The point-contact transistor was invented at Bell Labs in 1947. This semiconductor device helped enable smaller electronic systems compared with vacuum-tube equipment.

pages.title: Microprocessor, 1971
pages.body: Intel introduced the 4004 microprocessor in 1971. A microprocessor integrates processor functions on a semiconductor chip. This page concerns that historical introduction rather than current chip specifications.

pages.title: IBM PC, 1981
pages.body: IBM introduced its Personal Computer in 1981. The machine became an important part of personal computing history. This page does not describe every earlier personal computer.

pages.title: World Wide Web, 1989
pages.body: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989. The Web links information through hypertext. The Web is a service using the Internet, not a synonym for the Internet itself.
